issue: Where a jury's special-interrogatory answer finds drug quantity below a statutory threshold, may the sentencing judge find by a preponderance of the evidence a larger quantity that increases the sentence?
provision: 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1); Apprendi v. New Jersey, 530 U.S. 466 (2000)

sides.position: The jury's special-interrogatory finding is an affirmative finding of the actual drug quantity, so the judge cannot sentence on a higher quantity the jury did not find.
cases: United States v. Pimentel-Lopez, 859 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 2017)

sides.position: The special interrogatory only establishes the threshold the jury found beyond a reasonable doubt, and the judge may find a larger quantity at sentencing by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases: United States v. Smith, 751 F.3d 107 (3d Cir. 2014)
United States v. Webb, 545 F.3d 667 (8th Cir. 2008)
United States v. Magallanez, 408 F.3d 672 (10th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Leontaritis, 977 F.3d 447 (5th Cir. 2020)

this_court: Adopts the second position: the judge may find a quantity exceeding the jury's special-interrogatory threshold at sentencing (majority opinion, as characterized by the dissent).
quote: The upshot is that the majority opinion joins what I believe is the wrong side of a deeply entrenched circuit split, which has developed without careful parsing of the actual words of the relevant special interrogatories.
cite: United States v. John Leontaritis, 977 F.3d 447 (5th Cir. 2020)
